Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone.
  • Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care.
  • Sources indicate that we often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

The question is what happens next.

Sources indicate that we often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure, an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

Recent findings suggest that at first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: compassion unfolds within relationships.

In a recent development, during adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

Recent findings suggest that when educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on teaching empathy or kindness. Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as key. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

According to recent reports, in other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

According to recent reports, consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

Sources indicate that the question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

This perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Sources indicate that many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

According to recent reports, one of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Sources indicate that imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset, it’s navigating the delicate space between over-identifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

It has been revealed that people sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. Empathy allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. Compassion involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

According to recent reports, our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

For parents and educators, this finding has important practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

It has been revealed that in our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries key implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

In a recent development, young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

Industry observers note that this suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

There is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

Sources indicate that they unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

According to recent reports, when we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

It has been revealed that perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

Industry observers note that our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

Tyralynn Frazier, Ph.D., MPH, is an associate research scientist at Emory University’s Center for Contemplative Science and Compassion-Based Ethics. She leads international research in partnership with local collaborators, examining how social, emotional, and ethical (SEE) Learning and CBCT for Educators are implemented, adapted, and sustained across cultural contexts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal.

I think about this and a passage from Louise Erdrich’s 2005 novel The Painted Drum (public library) flits across the sky of my mind:.

Sources indicate that life will break you. Nobody can protect you from that, and living alone won’t either, for solitude will also break you with its yearning. You have to love. You have to feel. It is the reason you are here on earth. You are here to risk your heart. You are here to be swallowed up. And when it happens that you are broken, or betrayed, or left, or hurt, or death brushes near, let yourself sit by an apple tree and listen to the apples falling all around you in heaps, wasting their sweetness. Tell yourself that you tasted as many as you could.

Industry observers note that this, of course, is what life evolved to be — an aria of affirmation rising like luminous steam from the cold dark silence of an indifferent cosmos that will one day swallow all of it. Every living thing is its singer and its steward — something the poetic paleontologist Loren Eiseley captures with uncommon poignancy in his 1957 essay “The Judgment of the Birds,” found in his altogether magnificent posthumous collection The Star Thrower (public library).

Recent findings suggest that eiseley recounts resting beneath a tree after a day of trekking through fern and pine needles collecting fossils, dozing off in the warm sunlight, then being suddenly awakened by a great commotion to see “an enormous raven with a red and squirming nestling in his beak” perching on a crooked branch above. He writes:.

It has been revealed that into the glade fluttered small birds of half a dozen varieties drawn by the anguished outcries of the tiny parents. No one dared to attack the raven. But they cried there in some instinctive common misery, the bereaved and the unbereaved. The glade filled with their soft rustling and their cries. They fluttered as though to point their wings at the murderer. There was a dim intangible ethic he had violated, that they knew. He was a bird of death. And he, the murderer, the black bird at the heart of life, sat on there, glistening in the common light, formidable, unmoving, unperturbed, untouchable. The sighing died. It was then I saw the judgment. It was the judgment of life against death. I will never see it again so forcefully presented. I will never hear it again in notes so tragically prolonged. For in the midst of protest, they forgot the violence. There, in that clearing, the crystal note of a song sparrow lifted hesitantly in the hush. And finally, after painful fluttering, another took the song, and then another, the song passing from one bird to another, doubtfully at first, as though some evil thing were being slowly forgotten. Till suddenly they took heart and sang from many throats joyously together as birds are known to sing. They sang because life is sweet and sunlight beautiful. They sang under the brooding shadow of the raven. In simple truth they had forgotten the raven, for they were the singers of life, and not of death.

Couple with Hannah Arendt on love and how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the warblers and the wonder of being.

In a recent development, it was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the latest baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge.

It has been revealed that emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

Industry observers note that I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s notable to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

According to recent reports, emily came to see me for help with anxiety and insomnia, and a few sessions into our therapy she started to talk about memories that had been appearing for her, scenes from her childhood that suddenly had taken on fresh meaning or had popped up out of nowhere. It was as if her memories had changed, which made Emily feel crazy and even more anxious because she felt like she couldn’t trust herself anymore.

In the crudest terms, we tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet—a place where scenes, facts, annoying songs, and embarrassing moments are stored to be recalled, like when we try to remember what we had for dinner last week or where we went on holiday three years ago.

Sources indicate that when I talk about memory with my clients, they usually understand that it is not a perfect system, that it can alter over time and be very subjective. What is harder to convey is that decades of research suggest that memory is not in fact a filing cabinet or a library catalogue—it’s a construction. Every time I try to remember where we went on holiday three summers ago, my brain doesn’t retrieve but rather constructs a memory of our trip to Italy. That means that each time we recall something, that memory can change slightly or take on fresh meaning. Researchers Daniel L. Schacter and Donna Rose Addis found that, in fact, remembering and imagining look very similar in terms of activation in the brain.

It has been revealed that why does that matter? It can help make sense of what happened to Emily and what happens to many of my clients when they become parents and their relationships with their own parents change. Some of this is explained by a shift in roles: When a child becomes a parent, the dynamic of the child-parent relationship naturally has to change, which can be difficult for both parties. Grandparents and latest parents might find it challenging to adapt to who is in charge and “who knows best.” But sometimes the difficulty is more subtle, and it’s related to memory.

Emily struggled because she had started to have visceral memories of herself at about three to five years old, even though she had never actively thought about her childhood much before. She associated that phase in her life with a feeling of paralysis that she couldn’t explain. She told me how exhausted she felt every time she left her parents’ house now, like she had been holding her breath for hours.

According to recent reports, emily knew from whispered family stories that her mother had dealt with bouts of depression through much of her childhood. She also knew that her parents’ marriage hadn’t always been as placid and quiet as it was now. She had always had memories of them fighting late at night but had never thought much of it. Now she remembered her mother in tears, shouting and doors slamming. She remembered hiding under her bed.

Recent findings suggest that memory is heavily influenced by our current state of mind. Martin Conway, in his papers on autobiographical memory, explains that when we try to retrieve a memory or remember something spontaneously, we construct that memory in the moment, partly based on our current goals. If we are hungry, we might construct a memory of a cafe we saw on our walk two weeks ago. If we have a fight with our partner, we might suddenly remember all the times they disappointed us, when we usually are able to accept their imperfections.

When Emily became a parent, her goals changed dramatically, and it changed what memories her brain predicted might be useful for her.

Articles that explore holiday stress management, managing conflict, picking gifts, making resolutions, and more.

Industry observers note that emily realized that her experience of being her son’s age was one of bracing and zoning out because she had felt disconnected from her mother and scared of her father at the time. As a parent, Emily was suddenly able to attune to what it felt like for her to be three years old. Her three-year-old self did not feel safe, and she did not believe her child was safe, either.

According to recent reports, conway notes that the memories we are able to construct have to be coherent with how we think of ourselves, our beliefs about ourselves, and the world and people in it. According to Conway’s theory, our brains filter, rationalize, or dismiss memories that are inconsistent with who we believe we are.

It has been revealed that before Emily had children, she believed, largely unconsciously, that her childhood experiences were irrelevant to who she was and that she hadn’t really been affected by them. When she became a mum, her visceral memories of childhood fear did not match up with who she believed she was anymore. Her goals had changed from surviving and rationalizing to tuning in to and protecting her child. Her brain was telling her she had to shield her child from something that she had experienced as frightening as a child.

Other clients of mine have found that becoming a parent had the opposite effect. They were able to look at the younger versions of their parents with more compassion and kindness, reconstructing memories through the eyes of an exhausted parent who was trying and barely coping.

Recent findings suggest that karen and her parents had had a difficult relationship. Karen’s parents divorced when she was young, and Karen had always felt her mother had been unavailable when she was a child. She experienced a lot of anger when thinking about her childhood. She had memories of having to take on responsibilities too early, looking after her siblings, and cooking and cleaning while her mother was at work. Karen had purposefully moved away from her parents and had spent years asserting her independence. She had never wanted children because she had such strong memories of what it had been like to be a young caretaker and not being able to feel like a child. When she met her husband, she realized that creating her own family was more vital to her than she had thought.

Recent findings suggest that karen came to see me for anxiety. She was worried about losing her freedom when she became a mother, and we thought about how her childhood experiences shaped her experience now. I saw Karen for quite some time after she gave birth, and something shifted for her when she became a parent. She remembered instances of seeing her mother frazzled, rushed, and overwhelmed and how hard she had tried to find time to be there for Karen and her siblings. Karen started to realize how impossible it must have been for her mother to raise three children on her own while working.

Recent findings suggest that karen tried to talk to her mother and learned about how ashamed she was for burdening her daughter and unsure about whether Karen wanted her in her life. To her surprise, Karen experienced her mother’s relationship with her own daughter as reparative. She could make sense of her anger and her need for freedom and see that what happened in her childhood was not something her mother had intended.

According to recent reports, for Emily, too, her experiences meant she had to rebuild the relationship with her mother and find a more honest foundation. She was able to have conversations with her about what it would have been like for Emily growing up, and, to Emily’s surprise, her mother also listened and apologized for not having checked in with her sooner. It started a healing process for Emily that involved listening to what her three-year-old self might have felt and acknowledging that she had been trying to rationalize her way out of feeling for most of her life. She had to slowly let herself experience that her parents were safe now; she decided to not rely on them for child care but let the relationship grow more slowly.

According to recent reports, what helped Emily was hearing her mother validate what happened to her as a child. It was something Emily would have needed when she was younger. She was also able to make upcoming meaning of her relationship with her parents through therapy—an act of shared social construction with another human, the therapist, that fulfills some of our core needs of being heard, seen, and understood.

Karen similarly needed to feel heard by her mother. Her anger dissipated when she was able to put herself into her mother’s shoes and see that her and her mother’s experience could exist side by side.

What can you do if parenthood is shifting your relationship with your own parents? Here are steps that I have found are helpful for my clients.

Sources indicate that find support. The first step in coping with a difficult experience is to not try to go through it alone. We are social beings who need to feel understood by others. Seek out a friend or a sibling if you are struggling with feelings you do not understand.

Meet yourself with self-compassion. When strong emotions come up, we might tell ourselves, “I’m overreacting,” “I’m too sensitive,” “I just need to get on with things and stop complaining.” Self-criticism can perpetuate a cycle in which we invalidate our experiences until they become impossible to ignore. It also won’t help to be overly critical of yourself if you believe you’ve been judging your parents too harshly, now that you have the perspective of being a parent yourself.

Seek out conversations. If thinking back on your childhood memories brings up a perspective change on your childhood, speak to your family, your parents or siblings, and learn about how they experienced that time and you as a child. It might help you feel more compassion with your parents who may have been struggling, and can also help you understand yourself better as a person.

Set boundaries, if needed. If memories from your childhood suddenly take on upcoming meaning, it might be important to think about boundaries and clear rules to set with your child’s grandparents. If you felt unsafe or uncomfortable as a child, it is OK to make it clear how you expect the adults in your child’s life to behave. This can, of course, be easier noted than done, and it can be useful to seek help to deal with feelings of guilt or anxiety around setting boundaries with your parents.

Seek out professional help. Remember that every experience is subjective—your version of what happened might be different from that of your siblings or your parents. That does not make it any less valid. While Emily was lucky that her mother acknowledged her experience, your family members might not always be so receptive and might be more defensive about any wrongdoing. Seeking professional help can be especially useful when you are dealing with a family system that is less likely to take responsibility or want to change.

In a recent development, becoming a parent changes your world in a thousand ways and can dramatically alter the way you look at your own childhood. Self-compassion is hugely notable in navigating all the transformations you might go through as a new parent. Finding others that meet you with understanding and care is the first step in making sure you can meet yourself and your child in the same way.

*The stories in this article are a combination of experiences of several clients; any identifying information has been changed.

Sarah Emmerson, PsychD, is a chartered counseling psychologist and cofounder of Talking Women, a private psychology practice in London specializing in women's mental health.

Industry News: Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that “Every true theorist is a kind of tamed metaphysicist,” Einstein wrote as he contemplated the human passion for comprehension in the final years of his life.
  • In a recent development, no one studying this mature, grandly conceived work could believe that the author is a man of 21.
  • According to recent reports, indeed, this uncommon fusion of psychological acumen and scientific rigor only intensified as Pauli grew older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Every true theorist is a kind of tamed metaphysicist,” Einstein wrote as he contemplated the human passion for comprehension in the final years of his life. He may well have been thinking about the great Austrian-Swiss theoretical physicist Wolfgang Pauli (April 25, 1900–December 15, 1958), who first postulated the neutrino and was awarded the Nobel Prize for his discovery of the Pauli exclusion principle — a monumental leap in our understanding of the structure of matter. Decades earlier, 21-year-old Pauli had published a critique of Einstein’s groundbreaking theory of general relativity. It greatly impressed the elder physicist, who wrote in astonishment:.

In a recent development, no one studying this mature, grandly conceived work could believe that the author is a man of 21. One wonders what to admire most, the psychological understanding for the development of ideas, the sureness of mathematical deduction, the profound physical insight, the capacity for lucid systematic presentation, the complete treatment of the subject matter, or the sureness of critical appraisal.

According to recent reports, indeed, this uncommon fusion of psychological acumen and scientific rigor only intensified as Pauli grew older. Around the time he wrote the paper that spurred Einstein’s praise, Pauli became enchanted with the work of pioneering psychologist William James. After a three-decade immersion in it, and several years after he won the Nobel Prize in Physics, Pauli met the great psychiatrist Carl Jung (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who in turn was deeply influenced by Einstein’s ideas about space and time.

Jung and Pauli struck an unusual friendship, which lasted a quarter century until Pauli’s death and resulted in the invention of synchronicity — acausally connected events, which the observer experiences as having a meaningful connection on the basis of his or her subjective situation, a meeting point of internal and external reality.

Sources indicate that although rooted in Pauli’s interest in dream analysis, their conversations and correspondence went on to explore fundamental questions regarding the nature of reality through the dual lens of physics and psychology. Each used the tools of his expertise to shift the shoreline between the known and the unknown, and together they found common ground in the analogy between the atom, with its nucleus and orbiting electrons, and the self, with its central conscious ego and its ambient unconscious.

Industry observers note that both men were deeply imprinted by this intellectual cross-pollination. In his posthumously published final work, Jung would write:.

We do not know whether what we on the empirical plane regard as physical may not, in the Unknown beyond our experience, be identical with what on this side of the border we distinguish from the physical as psychic. Though we know from experience that psychic processes are related to material ones, we are not in a position to say in what this relationship consists or how it is possible at all. Precisely because the psychic and the physical are mutually dependent it has often been conjectured that they may be identical somewhere beyond our present experience, though this certainly does not justify the arbitrary hypothesis of either materialism or spiritualism.

Pauli’s parallel curiosity about mind and matter is perhaps best articulated in by his friend and collaborator Werner Heisenberg — he of uncertainty principle fame — who would later write:.

Behind [Pauli’s] outward display of criticism and skepticism lay concealed a deep philosophical interest even in those dark areas of reality of the human mind which elude the grasp of reason. And while the power of fascination emanating from Pauli’s analyses of physical problems was admittedly due in some measure to the detailed and penetrating clarity of his formulations, the rest was derived from a constant contact with the field of creative processes, for which no rational formulation as yet exists.

In their conceptually daring correspondence, collected in Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters, 1932–1958 (public library), the two delve into these parallels between the physical and psychic dimensions of reality. In one of his early letters, Jung considers the analogy Pauli had proposed between the atomic nucleus and the self. He writes in the autumn of 1935:.

In a recent development, generally speaking, the unconscious is thought of as psychic matter in an individual. However, the self-representation drawn up by the unconscious of its central structure does not accord with this view, for everything points to the fact that the central structure of the collective unconscious cannot be fixed locally but is an ubiquitous existence identical to itself; it must not be seen in spatial terms and consequently, when projected onto space, is to be found everywhere in that space. I even have the feeling that this peculiarity applies to time as well as space… A biological analogy would be the functional structure of a termite colony, possessing only unconscious performing organs, whereas the center, to which all the functions of the parts are related, is invisible and not empirically demonstrable.

Industry observers note that the radioactive nucleus is an excellent symbol for the source of energy of the collective unconscious, the ultimate external stratum of which appears an individual consciousness. As a symbol, it indicates that consciousness does not grow out of any activity that is inherent to it; rather, it is constantly being produced by an energy that comes from the depths of the unconscious and has thus been depicted in the form of rays since time immemorial.

The center, or the nucleus, has always been for me a symbol of the totality of the psychic, as the conscious plus the unconscious, the center of which does not coincide with the ego as the center of consciousness, and consequently has always been perceived as being external.

Over the following few years, their correspondence focuses primarily on dream analysis — which both Jung and Pauli saw as a means of illuminating scientific motifs in Pauli’s work — but again and again they return to the symmetry of mind and matter. In a letter to Jung from the summer of 1937, Pauli jeers at the narrow materialism of his own field and calls for an openness to other forms of knowing:.

Most modern physics also lends itself to the symbolic representation of psychic processes, even down to the last detail. Of course, nothing is further from the thoughts of modern man than the idea of penetrating the secrets of matter in this way … since it seems to him that, relatively speaking, less research has been done on the soul, and it is less familiar than matter.

The following summer, 38-year-old Pauli writes:.

After a careful and critical appraisal of the many experiences and arguments, I have come to accept the existence of deeper spiritual layers that cannot be adequately defined by the conventional concept of time.

In 1947, when Jung decided to found an institute dedicated to this field of research, he asked Pauli — who had received the Nobel Prize a year and a half earlier — to be among its sponsors. The physicist gladly agreed. In a letter to Jung from that December, he noted that the parallels between their interests provide “serious evidence that what is developing is indicative of a close fusion of psychology with the scientific experience of the processes in the material physical world.” He peers into that shared future:.

It is probably a long journey, one we are only just setting out on, and it will especially entail, as a modifying factor, constant criticism of the space-time concept.

According to recent reports, space and time were virtually turned by Newton into God’s right hand (oddly enough, the position made vacant when he expelled the Son of God from there), and it needed an extraordinary mental effort to bring time and space back down from these Olympian heights. Going hand in hand with this, apparently, is the criticism of the basic idea of classical natural science, according to which it describes objective facts to such an extent that there is absolutely no link between them and the researcher (objectifiability of the phenomena independently of the way in which they are observed.).

Four decades before the revered physicist John Archibald Wheeler (who coined the term “black hole”) made his influential assertion that “this is a participatory universe [and] observer-participancy gives rise to information,” Pauli plants the seed of a grand question:.

Industry observers note that modern microphysics turns the observer once again into a little lord of creation in his microcosm, with the ability (at least partially) of freedom of choice and fundamentally uncontrollable effects on that which is being observed. But if these phenomena are dependent on how (with what experimental system) they are observed, then is it not possible that they are also phenomena (extra corpus) that depend on who observes them (i.e., on the nature of the psyche of the observer)? And if natural science, in pursuit of the ideal of determinism since Newton, has finally arrived at the stage of the fundamental “perhaps” of the statistical character of natural laws … then should there not be enough room for all those oddities that ultimately rob the distinction between “physics” and “psyche” of all its meaning…?

It has been revealed that if you turn Pauli’s words over in your mind for a few moments, you’d realize just how radical and enormous a proposition this is. Indeed, it was this letter that catalyzed the series of conversations in which Pauli and Jung came up with the concept of synchronicity — the ultimate dependency between the observer and the observed. By the fall of 1948, they were using the term regularly in their correspondence. In a letter from mid-1949, Jung writes to Pauli, enclosing a manuscript of his first paper on the subject:.

Quite a while ago, you encouraged me to write down my thoughts on synchronicity… Nowadays, physicists are the only people who are paying serious attention to such ideas.

A few days later, Pauli echoes this faith in interdisciplinary thinking by sharing with Jung one of his great intellectual influences:.

The idea of meaningful coincidence — i.e., simultaneous events not causally connected — was expressed very clearly by Schopenhauer in his essay “On the Apparent Design in the Fate of the Individual.”.

According to recent reports, this essay of Schopenhauer’s had a lasting and fascinating effect on me and seemed to be pointing the way to a fresh trend in natural sciences. But whereas [he] wanted at all costs to cling to the rigid determinism along the lines of the classical physics of his day, we have now acknowledged that in the nuclear world, physical events cannot be followed in causal chains through time and space. Thus, the readiness to adopt the idea on which your work is based, that of the “meaning as an ordering factor,” is probably considerably greater among physicists than it was in Schopenhauer’s day.

In a subsequent letter from the autumn of 1950, Pauli — who preferred the term “meaning-correspondence” over “synchronicity” as a way of placing greater emphasis on the meaning of events than on their simultaneity — adds:.

In truth, nature is so fashioned that — analogous to Bohr’s “Complementarity” in physics — any contradiction between causality and synchronically can never be ascertained…. How do the facts that make up modern quantum physics relate to those other phenomena explained by you with the aid of the new principle of synchronicity? First of all, what is certain is that both types of phenomenon go beyond the framework of “classical” determinism.

I nevertheless, as a physicist, have the impression that the “statistical correspondence” of quantum physics, seen from the point of view of synchronicity, is a very weak generalization of the old causality… Although microphysics allows for an acausal form of observation, it actually has no use for the concept of “meaning.”.

In the letter, Pauli diagrams the concepts discussed:.

Six days later, Jung picks up the thread and crystallizes the definition of synchronicity:.

Synchronicity could be understood as an ordering system by means of which “similar” things coincide, without there being any apparent cause.

With an eye to Pauli’s diagram, he considers the role of space and time in synchronicity:.

Recent findings suggest that modern physics, having advanced into another world beyond conceivability, cannot dispense with the concept of a space-time continuum. Insofar as psychology penetrates into the unconscious, it probably has no alternative but to acknowledge the “indistinctness” or the impossibility of distinguishing between time and space, as well as their psychic relativity. The world of classical physics has not ceased to exist, and by the same token, the world of consciousness has not lost its validity against the unconscious… “Causality” is a psychologem (and originally a magic virtus) that formulates the connection between events and illustrates them as cause and effect. Another (incommensurable) approach that does the same thing in a different way is synchronicity. Both are identical in the higher sense of the term “connection” or “attachment.” But on the empirical and practical level (i.e., in the real world), they are incommensurable and antithetical, like space and time.

I would now like to propose that instead of “causality” we have “(relatively) constant connection through effect,” and instead of synchronicity we have (relatively) constant connection through contingency, equivalence, or “meaning.”.

He illustrates this proposition with his own variation on Pauli’s diagram:.

In a letter sent twelve days later, Pauli responds by introducing the crucial concept of scale into these considerations of synchronicity:.

Synchronicity should be defined in a narrower sense so as to comprise effects that only appear when there is a small number of individual cases but disappear when there is a larger number… In quantum physics, there are not just effects that appear with large numbers instead of with small ones, and not only is the term “meaning” not the right one here (which you have written about at great length) but also the concept of the (psychic or psychoid) archetype cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

In a letter from October of 1953, more than twenty years into their correspondence and a decade into their shared obsession with synchronicity, Jung writes to Pauli:.

Recent findings suggest that it means a lot to me to see how our points of view are getting closer, for if you feel isolated from your contemporaries when grappling with the unconscious, it is also the same with me, in fact more so, since I am actually standing in the isolated area, striving somehow to bridge the gap that separates me from the others. After all, it is no pleasure for me always to be regarded as esoteric. Oddly enough, the problem is still the same 2,000-year-old one: How does one get from Three to Four?

In a recent development, jung and Pauli unfurl many more fascinating parallels between psychology and physics in the remainder of Atom and Archetype. Complement it with Jung on human nature, then revisit physicist, novelist, and poet Alan Lightman on science and transcendence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.

It has been revealed that alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.

Recent findings suggest that many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.

A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once said to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.

Winifred Nicholson’s Seascape with Two Boats (1932) Photo: © Kettle’s Yard, University of Cambridge; © Trustees of Winifred Nicholson.

The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.

Scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.

The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a latest direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott says, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.

It has been revealed that scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”.

• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, my father was a joyful individual who had the sweetest smile and distinct laugh. His favorite color was blue. Industry News: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades.
  • Sources indicate that as the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an notable public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020. What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017.

Sources indicate that as the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens looks to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

In a recent development, the ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she mentioned. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”.

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall. Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she remarked.

According to recent reports, it’s easy to talk about structural racism as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together worsened suicide risk for Black young adults.

Recent findings suggest that brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she stated. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

Recent findings suggest that when she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

According to recent reports, “We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she stated. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

In a recent development, brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).

As a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention. It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens remarked.

Already, in a study from 2023, she and her colleagues indicated that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified mindfulness and meditation as potential tools for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk.

This approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens stated. When a child shows signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place.

And, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens stated that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

Sources indicate that “It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she said. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”.

#10371. J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2707 w)

J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,” the great Maurice Sendak once stated in an interview.
  • Industry observers note that on March 8, 1939, J.R.R.
  • Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,” the great Maurice Sendak once stated in an interview. “I don’t write for children,” he told Colbert. “I write — and somebody claims, ‘That’s for children!’” This sentiment — the idea that designating certain types of literature as “children’s” is a choice entirely arbitrary and entirely made by adults — has since been eloquently echoed by Neil Gaiman, but isn’t, in fact, a new idea.

Industry observers note that on March 8, 1939, J.R.R. Tolkien (January 3, 1892–September 2, 1973), celebrated as one of the greatest fantasy writers in history, gave a lecture titled “Fairy Stories,” eventually adapted into an essay retitled “On Fairy-Stories” and included in the appendix to Tales from the Perilous Realm (public library). At the crux of his argument, which explores the nature of fantasy and the cultural role of fairy tales, is the same profound conviction that there is no such thing as writing “for children.”.

Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:.

A “fairy-story” is one which touches on or uses Faerie, whatever its own main purpose may be: satire, adventure, morality, fantasy. Faerie itself may perhaps most nearly be translated by Magic — but it is magic of a peculiar mood and power, at the furthest pole from the vulgar devices of the laborious, scientific, magician. There is one proviso: if there is any satire present in the tale, one thing must not be made fun of, the magic itself. That must in that story be taken seriously, neither laughed at nor explained away.

He then explores the relationship between fairy tales and language, denouncing Max Müller’s view of mythology as a “disease of language”:.

Mythology is not a disease at all, though it may like all human things become diseased. You might as well say that thinking is a disease of the mind. It would be more near the truth to say that languages, especially modern European languages, are a disease of mythology. But Language cannot, all the same, be dismissed. The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale are in our world coeval. The human mind, endowed with the powers of generalization and abstraction, sees not only green-grass, discriminating it from other things (and finding it fair to look upon), but sees that it is green as well as being grass. But how powerful, how stimulating to the very faculty that produced it, was the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent. And that is not surprising: such incantations might indeed be stated to be only another view of adjectives, a part of speech in a mythical grammar. The mind that thought of light, heavy, grey, yellow, still, swift, also conceived of magic that would make heavy things light and able to fly, turn grey lead into yellow gold, and the still rock into a swift water. If it could do the one, it could do the other; it inevitably did both. When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter’s power — upon one plane; and the desire to wield that power in the world external to our minds awakes. It does not follow that we shall use that power well upon any plane. We may put a deadly green upon a man’s face and produce a horror; we may make the rare and terrible blue moon to shine; or we may cause woods to spring with silver leaves and rams to wear fleeces of gold, and put hot fire into the belly of the cold worm. But in such “fantasy,” as it is called, upcoming form is made; Faerie begins; Man becomes a sub-creator.

Like Sendak and Gaiman, Tolkien insists that fairy tales aren’t inherently “for” children but that we, as adults, simply decide that they are, based on a series of misconceptions about both the nature of this literature and the nature of children:.

It is usually assumed that children are the natural or the specially appropriate audience for fairy-stories. In describing a fairy-story which they think adults might possibly read for their own entertainment, reviewers frequently indulge in such waggeries as: “this book is for children from the ages of six to sixty.” But I have never yet seen the puff of a fresh motor-model that began thus: “this toy will amuse infants from seventeen to seventy”; though that to my mind would be much more appropriate. Is there any essential connexion between children and fairy-stories? Is there any call for comment, if an adult reads them for himself? Reads them as tales, that is, not studies them as curios. Adults are allowed to collect and study anything, even old theatre programmes or paper bags.

Among those who still have enough wisdom not to think fairy-stories pernicious, the common opinion seems to be that there is a natural connexion between the minds of children and fairy-stories, of the same order as the connexion between children’s bodies and milk. I think this is an error; at best an error of false sentiment, and one that is therefore most often made by those who, for whatever private reason (such as childlessness), tend to think of children as a special kind of creature, almost a different race, rather than as normal, if immature, members of a particular family, and of the human family at large.

He argues, instead, that the stereotype of fairy tales being associated with children and native to their world is “an accident of our domestic history”:.

Recent findings suggest that fairy-stories have in the modern lettered world been relegated to the “nursery,” as shabby or old-fashioned furniture is relegated to the play-room, primarily because the adults do not want it, and do not mind if it is misused. It is not the choice of the children which decides this. Children as a class—except in a common lack of experience they are not one—neither like fairy-stories more, nor understand them better than adults do; and no more than they like many other things. They are young and growing, and normally have keen appetites, so the fairy-stories as a rule go down well enough. But in fact only some children, and some adults, have any special taste for them; and when they have it, it is not exclusive, nor even necessarily dominant. It is a taste, too, that would not appear, I think, very early in childhood without artificial stimulus; it is certainly one that does not decrease but increases with age, if it is innate.

According to recent reports, the nursery and schoolroom are merely given such tastes and glimpses of the adult thing as seem fit for them in adult opinion (often much mistaken). Any one of these things would, if left altogether in the nursery, become gravely impaired. So would a beautiful table, a good picture, or a useful machine (such as a microscope), be defaced or broken, if it were left long unregarded in a schoolroom. Fairy-stories banished in this way, cut off from a full adult art, would in the end be ruined; indeed in so far as they have been so banished, they have been ruined.

Tolkien then moves on to the subject of fantasy, a frequently misunderstood faculty of the imagination.

According to recent reports, the mental power of image-making is one thing, or aspect; and it should appropriately be called Imagination. The perception of the image, the grasp of its implications, and the control, which are necessary to a successful expression, may vary in vividness and strength: but this is a difference of degree in Imagination, not a difference in kind. The achievement of the expression, which gives (or seems to give) “the inner consistency of reality,” is indeed another thing, or aspect, needing another name: Art, the operative link between Imagination and the final result, Sub-creation. For my present purpose I require a word which shall embrace both the Sub- creative Art in itself and a quality of strangeness and wonder in the Expression, derived from the Image: a quality essential to fairy-story. I propose, therefore, to arrogate to myself the powers of Humpty-Dumpty, and to use Fantasy for this purpose: in a sense, that is, which combines with its older and higher use as an equivalent of Imagination the derived notions of “unreality” (that is, of unlikeness to the Primary World), of freedom from the domination of observed “fact,” in short of the fantastic. I am thus not only aware but glad of the etymological and semantic connexions of fantasy with fantastic: with images of things that are not only “not actually present,” but which are indeed not to be found in our primary world at all, or are generally believed not to be found there. But while admitting that, I do not assent to the depreciative tone. That the images are of things not in the primary world (if that indeed is possible) is a virtue, not a vice. Fantasy (in this sense) is, I think, not a lower but a higher form of Art, indeed the most nearly pure form, and so (when achieved) the most potent.

He goes on to argue that, despite the many misconceptions that envelop it, fantasy is far more challenging an art than nonfiction, for it necessitates the creation of an elaborate, immersive world from scratch, without the crutch of reality:.

In a recent development, fantasy … is difficult to achieve. Fantasy may be, as I think, not less but more sub-creative; but at any rate it is found in practice that “the inner consistency of reality” is more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images and the rearrangements of primary material to the actual arrangements of the Primary World. It is easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material. Fantasy thus, too often, remains undeveloped; it is and has been used frivolously, or only half-seriously, or merely for decoration: it remains merely “fanciful.” Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun. Many can then imagine or picture it. But that is not enough — though it may already be a more potent thing than many a “thumbnail sketch” or “transcript of life” that receives literary praise.

Recent findings suggest that to make a Secondary World inside which the green sun will be credible, commanding Secondary Belief, will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill, a kind of elvish craft. Few attempt such difficult tasks. But when they are attempted and in any degree accomplished then we have a rare achievement of Art: indeed narrative art, story-making in its primary and most potent mode.

Tolkien makes a curious argument about the oil-and-water relationship between fantasy and drama, managing to slip in a subtle dig at none other than The Bard:.

According to recent reports, in human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature. … It is a misfortune that Drama, an art fundamentally distinct from Literature, should so commonly be considered together with it, or as a branch of it. Among these misfortunes we may reckon the depreciation of Fantasy. For in part at least this depreciation is due to the natural desire of critics to cry up the forms of literature or “imagination” that they themselves, innately or by training, prefer. And criticism in a country that has produced so great a Drama, and possesses the works of William Shakespeare, tends to be far too dramatic. But Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy. Fantasy, even of the simplest kind, hardly ever succeeds in Drama, when that is presented as it should be, visibly and audibly acted. Fantastic forms are not to be counterfeited. Men dressed up as talking animals may achieve buffoonery or mimicry, but they do not achieve Fantasy. . . .

Recent findings suggest that in Macbeth, when it is read, I find the witches tolerable: they have a narrative function and some hint of dark significance; though they are vulgarized, poor things of their kind. They are almost intolerable in the play. They would be quite intolerable, if I were not fortified by some memory of them as they are in the story as read. I am told that I should feel differently if I had the mind of the period, with its witch-hunts and witch-trials. But that is to say: if I regarded the witches as possible, indeed likely, in the Primary World; in other words, if they ceased to be “Fantasy.” That argument concedes the point. To be dissolved, or to be degraded, is the likely fate of Fantasy when a dramatist tries to use it, even such a dramatist as Shakespeare. Macbeth is indeed a work by a playwright who ought, at least on this occasion, to have written a story, if he had the skill or patience for that art.

Another misconception Tolkien debunks — speaking to Susan Sontag’s conviction that polarities only rob life of dimension — is the notion that the fantastical is somehow diametrically opposed to the rational:.

It has been revealed that fantasy is a natural human activity. It certainly does not destroy or even insult Reason; and it does not either blunt the appetite for, nor obscure the perception of, scientific verity. On the contrary. The keener and the clearer is the reason, the better fantasy will it make. If men were ever in a state in which they did not want to know or could not perceive truth (facts or evidence), then Fantasy would languish until they were cured. If they ever get into that state (it would not seem at all impossible), Fantasy will perish, and become Morbid Delusion.

For creative Fantasy is founded upon the hard recognition that things are so in the world as it appears under the sun; on a recognition of fact, but not a slavery to it. So upon logic was founded the nonsense that displays itself in the tales and rhymes of Lewis Carroll. If men really could not distinguish between frogs and men, fairy-stories about frog-kings would not have arisen.

Returning to his notion of the Secondary World driven by Secondary Belief, Tolkien contributes to history’s greatest definitions of art:.

Art is the human process that produces by the way (it is not its only or ultimate object) Secondary Belief.

He then adds to the psychological functions of art by exploring the psychological functions of fairy tales, chief among which is their capacity for rebooting our chronically blunted attention:.

Sources indicate that recovery (which includes return and renewal of health) is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view. I do not say “seeing things as they are” and involve myself with the philosophers, though I might venture to say “seeing things as we are (or were) meant to see them”—as things apart from ourselves. We need, in any case, to clean our windows; so that the things seen clearly may be freed from the drab blur of triteness or familiarity—from possessiveness. Of all faces those of our familiares are the ones both most difficult to play fantastic tricks with, and most difficult really to see with fresh attention, perceiving their likeness and unlikeness: that they are faces, and yet unique faces. This triteness is really the penalty of “appropriation”: the things that are trite, or (in a bad sense) familiar, are the things that we have appropriated, legally or mentally. We say we know them. They have become like the things which once attracted us by their glitter, or their colour, or their shape, and we laid hands on them, and then locked them in our hoard, acquired them, and acquiring ceased to look at them.

Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.

It has been revealed that the full fifteen-page essay, as well as the rest of Tales from the Perilous Realm, is well worth a read. Complement it with Tolkien’s little-known illustrations for the first edition of The Hobbit.
