💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that manners today are often seen as a quaint subject that belongs in Lord Chesterfield’s outlandish advice on the art of pleasing or Esquire‘s dated guide to dating.
  • Politeness has been defined as an “artificial good-nature;” but it would be better said that good-nature is natural politeness.
  • The true aim of politeness, is to make those with whom you associate as well satisfied with themselves as possible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that manners today are often seen as a quaint subject that belongs in Lord Chesterfield’s outlandish advice on the art of pleasing or Esquire‘s dated guide to dating. But in a culture where we regularly do online what we’d never do in person and behave offline in ways our grandparents wouldn’t have dared dream of even in their most defiant fantasies, there’s something to be said for the lost art of, if not “manners,” politeness and simple respect in communication. Though originally published in 1866, Martine’s Hand-book of Etiquette, and Guide to True Politeness (public library; public domain; free Kindle download) by Arthur Martine contains a treasure trove of timeless — and increasingly timely — pointers on the necessary art of living up to our social-animal destiny.

Martine contextualizes his mission:.

Politeness has been defined as an “artificial good-nature;” but it would be better said that good-nature is natural politeness. It inspires us with an unremitting attention, both to please others and to avoid giving them offense. Its code is a ceremonial, agreed upon and established among mankind, to give each other external testimonies of friendship or respect. Politeness and etiquette form a sort of supplement to the law, which enables society to protect itself against offenses which the law cannot touch. For instance, the law cannot punish a man for habitually staring at people in an insolent and annoying manner, but etiquette can banish such an offender from the circles of good society, and fix upon him the brand of vulgarity. Etiquette consists in certain forms, ceremonies, and rules which the principle of politeness establishes and enforces for the regulation of the manners of men and women in their intercourse with each other.

The true aim of politeness, is to make those with whom you associate as well satisfied with themselves as possible. … Politeness is a sort of social benevolence, which avoids wounding the pride, or shocking the prejudices of those around you.

But he offers an crucial disclaimer:.

It has been revealed that [Politeness] must be cultivated, for the promptings of nature are eminently selfish, and courtesy and good-breeding are only attainable by effort and discipline. But even courtesy has limits where dignity should govern it, for when carried to excess, particularly in manner, it borders on sycophancy, which is almost as despicable as rudeness. To overburden people with attention; to render them uncomfortable with a prodigality of proffered services; to insist upon obligations which they do not desire, is not only to render yourself disagreeable, but contemptible.

Among Martine’s most timeless advice are his guidelines on the art of conversation, to which an entire section of the book is dedicated. He begins:.

In a recent development, as the object of conversation is pleasure and improvement, those subjects only which are of universal interest can be made legitimate topics of pleasantry or discussion. And it is the gift of expressing thoughts and fancies in a quick, brilliant, and graceful manner on such topics,—of striking out fresh ideas, eliciting the views and opinions of others, of attaching the interest of all to the subject discussed, giving it, however trifling in itself, weight and importance in the estimation of the hearers, that constitutes the great talent for conversation. But this talent can never, we may safely aver, be displayed except in a good cause, and when conversation is carried on in a spirit of genuine charity and benevolence.

It has been revealed that the power of preserving silence is the very first requisite to all who wish to shine, or even please in discourse; and those who cannot preserve it, have really no business to speak. … The silence that, without any deferential air, listens with polite attention, is more flattering than compliments, and more frequently broken for the purpose of encouraging others to speak, than to display the listener’s own powers. This is the really eloquent silence. It requires great genius—more perhaps than speaking—and few are gifted with the talent….

Industry observers note that never give short or sharp answers in ordinary conversation, unless you aspire to gain distinction by mere rudeness; for they have in fact no merit, and are only uncivil. “I do not know,” “I cannot tell,” are the most harmless words possible, and may yet be rendered very offensive by the tone and manner in which they are pronounced. Never reply, in answer to a question like the following, “Did Mrs. Spitewell tell you how Miss Rosebud’s marriage was getting on?” “I did not ask.” It is almost like saying, I never ask impertinent questions, though you do; we learn plenty of things in the world without having first inquired about them. If you must say, you did not ask, say, that “you forgot to ask,” “neglected it,” or “did not think of it.” We can always be ordinarily civil, even if we cannot always be absolutely wise.

Leave quibbling of every kind to lawyers pleading at the bar for the life of a culprit; in society and conversation it is invariably out of place, unless when Laughter is going his merry round. At all other times it is a proof of bad breeding.

He then goes on to outline a cautionary taxonomy of “bores” and other ill-mannered conversation archetypes, diagnosing the specific downfall of each:.

Sources indicate that all subjects are alike to him; he speaks on every topic with equal fluency, is never at a loss, quotes high authority for every assertion, and allows no one else to utter a word; he silences, without the least ceremony, every attempt at interruption, however cleverly managed. … Great, and especially loud and positive talkers, have been denounced by all writers on manners as shallow and superficial persons.

Recent findings suggest that [This is] the man who gives an account of his dogs, horses, lands, books, and pictures. Whatever is his, must, he thinks, interest others; and listen they must, however resolutely they may attempt to change the current of his discourse.

In a recent development, women of this class are sometimes too fond of praising their children. It is no doubt an amiable weakness; but I would still advise them to indulge as little as possible in the practice; for however dear the rosy-cheeked, curly-headed prattlers may be to them, the chances are, that others will vote the darlings to be great bores; you that have children, never speak of them in company.

The grave expounder of truisms belongs to this class. He cannot allow the simplest conversation to go on, without entering into proofs and details familiar to every child nine years of age; and the tenor of his discourse, however courteous in terms and manner, pays you the very indifferent compliment, of supposing that you have fallen from some other planet, in total and absolute ignorance of the most ordinary and every-day things connected with this little world of ours. All foreigners are particularly great at this style of boring.

Sources indicate that if he refrains from the direct and absolute rudeness of yawning in your face, [he] reveals, by short and drawling answers, given at fits and starts, and completely at variance with the object of the conversation, that he affects at least a total indifference to the party present, and to the subject of discourse. In society, the absent man is uncivil; he who affects to be so, is rude and vulgar. All persons who speak of their ailings, diseases, or bodily infirmities, are offensive bores. Subjects of this sort should be addressed to doctors, who are paid for listening to them, and to no one else. Bad taste is the failing of these bores.

[These are] the ladies and gentlemen who pay long visits, and who, meeting you at the door prepared to sally forth, keep you talking near the fire till the beauty of the day is passed; and then take their leave, “hoping they have not detained you.” Bad feeling or want of tact here predominates.

In a recent development, [They] constantly speak on the same eternal subject [and] bore you at all times and at all hours, whether you are in health or in sickness, in spirits or in sorrow, with the same endless topic, must not be overlooked in our list; though it is sufficient to denounce them. Their failing is occasioned by a total want of judgment.

A numerous and unhappy family [who] are constantly addressing the most unsuitable speeches to individuals or parties. To the blind they will speak of fine pictures and scenery; and will entertain a person in deep mourning with the anticipated pleasures of to-morrow’s ball. A total want of ordinary thought and observation, is the general cause of the Malaprop failing.

It is truly revolting, indeed, to approach the very Boa-constrictor of good society; the snake who comes upon us, not in the natural form of a huge, coarse, slow reptile, but Proteus-like, in a thousand different forms; though all displaying at the first sight the boa-bore, ready to slime over every subject of discourse with the vile saliva of selfish vanity. Pah! it is repulsive even to speak of the species, numerous, too, as the sands along the shore.

Martine adds an admonition against talking too much by way of Jonathan Swift, who observed:.

Industry observers note that nothing is more generally exploded than the folly of talking too much; yet I rarely remember to have seen five people together, where some one among them hath not been predominant in that kind, to the great constraint and disgust of all the rest. But among such as deal in multitudes of words, none are comparable to the sober, deliberate talker, who proceedeth with much thought and caution, maketh his preface, brancheth out into several digressions, findeth a hint that putteth him in mind of another story, which he promises to tell you when this is done, cometh back regularly to his subject, cannot readily call to mind some person’s name, holdeth his head, complaineth of his memory; the whole company all this while in suspense; at last says, it is no matter, and so goes on. And to crown the business, it perhaps proveth at last a story the company has heard fifty times before, or at best some insipid adventure of the relater.

He then offers his own counsel on striking the right balance:.

In conversation there must be, as in love and in war, some hazarding, some rattling on; nor need twenty falls affect you, so long as you take cheerfulness and good humor for your guides; but the careful and measured conversation just described is always, though perfectly correct, extremely dull and tedious — a vast blunder from first to last.

Sources indicate that the great charm of conversation consists less in the display of one’s own wit and intelligence, than in the power to draw forth the resources of others; he who leaves you after a long conversation, pleased with himself and the part he has taken in the discourse, will be your warmest admirer. Men do not care to admire you, they wish you to be pleased with them; they do not seek for instruction or even amusement from your discourse, but they do wish you to be made acquainted with their talents and powers of conversation; and the true man of genius will delicately make all who come in contact with him feel the exquisite satisfaction of knowing that they have appeared to advantage.

Of the vanity of knowledge — which makes it tempting to learn to talk about books you haven’t read — Martine observes:.

No, no, let us not deceive ourselves; we never want subjects of conversation; but we often want the knowledge how to treat them; above all, how to bring them forward in a graceful and pleasing manner.

He then recapitulates the essence of the art of conversation:.

Recent findings suggest that cheerfulness, unaffected cheerfulness, a sincere desire to please and be pleased, unchecked by any efforts to shine, are the qualities you must bring with you into society, if you wish to succeed in conversation. … a light and airy equanimity of temper,—that spirit which never rises to boisterousness, and never sinks to immovable dullness; that moves gracefully from “grave to gay, from serious to serene,” and by mere manner gives proof of a feeling heart and generous mind.

According to recent reports, the chapter ends with some “general rules for conversation,” in which Martine presents a selection of do’s and don’ts. Here is a synthesis of his most salient points:.

Reproof is a medicine like mercury or opium; if it be improperly administered, with report either to the adviser or the advised, it will do harm instead of good.

If a man is telling that which is as old as the hills, or which you believe to be false, the better way is to let him go on. Why should you refuse a man the pleasure of believing that he is telling you something which you never heard before? Besides, by refusing to believe him, or by telling him that his story is old, you not only mortify him, but the whole manufacturer is made uneasy, and, by sympathy, share his mortification.

According to recent reports, it is bad manners to satirize lawyers in the presence of lawyers, or doctors in the presence of one of that calling, and so of all the professions. Nor should you rail against bribery and corruption in the presence of politicians, (especially of a Fresh York politician,) or members of Congress, as they will have good reason to suppose that you are hinting at them. It is the aim of politeness to leave the arena of social intercourse untainted with any severity of language, or bitterness of feeling.

It has been revealed that whenever the lady or gentleman with whom you are discussing a point, whether of love, war, science or politics, begins to sophisticate, drop the subject instantly. Your adversary either wants the ability to maintain his opinion,– and then it would be uncivil to press it — or he wants the still more useful ability to yield the point with unaffected grace and good-humor; or what is also possible, his vanity is in some way engaged in defending views on which he may probably have acted, so that to demolish his opinions is perhaps to reprove his conduct, and no well-bred man goes into society for the purpose of sermonizing.

To reprove with success, the following circumstances are necessary, viz.: mildness, secrecy, intimacy, and the esteem of the person you would reprove.

If you have been once in organization with an idle person, it is enough. You need never go again. You have heard all he knows. And he has had no opportunity of learning anything fresh. For idle people make no improvements.

Don’t give your time to every superficial acquaintance: it is bestowing what is to you of inestimable worth, upon one who is not likely to be the better for it.

Be careful of your word, even in keeping the most trifling appointment. But do not blame another for a failure of that kind, till you have heard his excuse.

All local wits, all those whose jests are understood only within the range of their own circle or coterie, are decided objectionables in general society. It is the height of ill-breeding, in fact, to converse, or jest, on subjects that are not perfectly understood by the party at large; it is a species of rude mystification, as uncivil as whispering, or as speaking in language that may not be familiar to some of the party. But you must not make a fool of yourself, even if others show themselves deficient in good manners; and must not, like inflated simpletons, fancy yourself the object of every idle jest you do not understand, or of every laugh that chance may have called forth. Ladies and gentlemen feel that they are neither laughed at nor ridiculed.

In society, the object of conversation is of course entertainment and improvement, and it must, therefore, be adapted to the circle in which it is carried on, and must be neither too high nor too deep for the party at large, so that every one may contribute his share, just at his pleasure, and to the best of his ability.

A gentleman will, by all means, avoid showing his learning and accomplishments in the presence of ignorant and vulgar people, who can, by no possibility, understand or appreciate them. It is a pretty sure sign of bad breeding to set people to staring and feeling uncomfortable.

In a mixed company, never speak to your friend of a matter which the rest do not understand, unless it is something which you can explain to them, and which may be made interesting to the whole party.

Sources indicate that do not endeavor to shine in all companies. Leave room for your hearers to imagine something within you beyond all you have noted.

Recent findings suggest that think like the wise; but talk like ordinary people. Never go out of the common road, but for somewhat.

Put yourself on the same level as the person to whom you speak, and under penalty of being considered a pedantic idiot, refrain from explaining any expression or word that you may use.

According to recent reports, you need not tell all the truth, unless to those who have a right to know it all. But let all you tell be truth.

Industry observers note that if a favor is asked of you, grant it, if you can. If not, refuse it in such a manner, as that one denial may be sufficient.

Fools pretend to foretell what will be the concern of things, and are laughed at for their awkward conjectures. Wise men, being aware of the uncertainty of human affairs, and having observed how small a matter often produces a great change, are modest in their conjectures.

According to recent reports, reflect upon the different appearances things make to you from what they did some years ago, and don’t imagine that your opinion will never alter, because you are extremely positive at present. Let the remembrance of your past changes of sentiment make you more flexible.

Recent findings suggest that in disputes upon moral or scientific points, ever let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.

Give your opinion modestly, but freely; hear that of others with candor; and ever endeavor to find out, and to communicate truth.

It has been revealed that it is an advantage to have concealed one’s opinion. For by that means you may change your judgment of things (which every wise man finds reason to do) and not be accused of fickleness.

Recent findings suggest that avoid the habit of employing French words in English conversation; it is extremely bad taste to be always using such expressions as ci-devant, soi-disant, en masse, couleur de rose, etc. Do not salute your acquaintances with bon jour, nor reply to every proposition, volontiers.

There is an affected humility more insufferable than downright pride, as hypocrisy is more abominable than libertinism. Take care that your virtues be genuine and unsophisticated.

Recent findings suggest that if you can express yourself to be perfectly understood in ten words, never use a dozen. Go not about to prove, by a long series of reasoning, what all the world is ready to own.

Recent findings suggest that you will please so much the less, if you go into company determined to shine. Let your conversation appear to rise out of thoughts suggested by the occasion, not strained or premeditated: nature always pleases: affectation is always odious.

Nothing is more nauseous than apparent self-sufficiency. For it shows the tech giant two things, which are extremely disagreeable: that you have a high opinion of yourself, and that you have comparatively a mean opinion of them.

The modest man is seldom the object of envy.

In a recent development, if you are really a wit, remember that in conversation its true office consists more in finding it in others, than showing off a great deal of it yourself. He who goes out of your company pleased with himself is sure to be pleased with you.

Recent findings suggest that martine’s Hand-book of Etiquette, and Guide to True Politeness is a treat in its entirety. It’s available as a free download in multiple formats from Project Gutenberg, or as a cleaned up and formatted free Kindle book.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while looks continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.

While most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly released, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebranding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly revealed Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.

Frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh. “It’s a marriage,” Nusseibeh states about the fair’s partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism. “And the fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding” Courtesy Frieze Abu Dhabi.

Regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo demonstrates at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.

In a recent development, this market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.

"We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh notes. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market.".

Industry observers note that that step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh notes, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.

Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the organization following a growing market. “Our last newly introduced fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”.

Frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a latest collecting cohort.

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, scheduled to open on 11 December, is in Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District Courtesy the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the company run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a new company founded by Emanuel called Mari.

Mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of the DCT’s chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.

Industry observers note that this multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. It should also ensure Frieze's intends align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.

Zayed National Museum opened in December 2025 Courtesy Zayed National Museum.

In a recent development, the arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.

According to recent reports, how measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no intends to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.

In a recent development, the luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

Stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.

The fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, long before there was Yo-Yo Ma, there was Spanish Catalan cellist and conductor Pablo Casals (December 29, 1876–October 22, 1973), regarded by many — including Yo-Yo Ma — as the greatest cellist of all time. The recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the U.N. Peace Medal for his unflinching dedication to justice and his lifelong stance against oppression and dictatorship, Casals was as much an extraordinary artist as he was an extraordinary human being — a generous and kind man of uncommon compassion and goodness of heart, a passionate spirit in love with life, and an unflinching idealist.

Sources indicate that and yet, like many exceptional people, he cultivated his character through an early brush with suffering. In his late teenage years, already a celebrated prodigy, he underwent an anguishing spiritual crisis of the kind Tolstoy faced in his later years and came close to suicide. But with the loving support of his mother, he regained his center and went on to become a man of great talent, great accomplishment, and great vitality.

To mark his ninetieth birthday, Casals began a collaboration with photojournalist Albert E. Kahn that would eventually become the 1970 autobiography-of-sorts Joys and Sorrows (public library) — one of the most magnificent perspectives of the creative life ever committed to words.

Straight from the opening, Casals cracks open the essence of his extraordinary character and the source of his exuberant life-energy with a beautiful case for how purposeful work is the true fountain of youth:.

On my last birthday I was ninety-three years old. That is not young, of course. In fact, it is older than ninety. But age is a relative matter. If you continue to work and to absorb the beauty in the world about you, you find that age does not necessarily mean getting old. At least, not in the ordinary sense. I feel many things more intensely than ever before, and for me life grows more fascinating.

Recounting being at once delighted and unsurprised by an article in the London Sunday Times about an orchestra in the Caucasus composed of musicians older than a hundred, he considers the spring of their vitality:.

Sources indicate that in spite of their age, those musicians have not lost their zest for life. How does one explain this? I do not think the answer lies simply in their physical constitutions or in something unique about the climate in which they live. It has to do with their attitude toward life; and I believe that their ability to work is due in no small measure to the fact that they do work. Work helps prevent one from getting old. I, for one, cannot dream of retiring. Not now or ever. Retire? The word is alien and the idea inconceivable to me. I don’t believe in retirement for anyone in my type of work, not while the spirit remains. My work is my life. I cannot think of one without the other. To “retire” means to me to begin to die. The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age. Each day I am reborn. Each day I must begin again.

For the past eighty years I have started each day in the same manner.

With great elegance, he contrasts the dullness of mindless routine with the exhilaration of mindful ritual — something many great artists engineer into their days. In a sentiment Henry Miller would come to echo only two years later in his own memorable meditation on the secret of remaining forever young, Casals writes of his daily practice:.

Recent findings suggest that it is not a mechanical routine but something essential to my daily life. I go to the piano, and I play two preludes and fugues of Bach. I cannot think of doing otherwise. It is a sort of benediction on the house. But that is not its only meaning for me. It is a rediscovery of the world of which I have the joy of being a part. It fills me with awareness of the wonder of life, with a feeling of the incredible marvel of being a human being. The music is never the same for me, never. Each day is something fresh, fantastic, unbelievable. That is Bach, like nature, a miracle!

Casals, indeed, finds great vitalization in bearing witness to nature’s mastery of the self-renewal so essential for the human spirit over the long run:.

I do not think a day passes in my life in which I fail to look with fresh amazement at the miracle of nature. It is there on every side. It can be simply a shadow on a mountainside, or a spider’s web gleaming with dew, or sunlight on the leaves of a tree. I have always especially loved the sea. Whenever possible, I have lived by the sea… It has long been a custom of mine to walk along the beach each morning before I start to work. True, my walks are shorter than they used to be, but that does not lessen the wonder of the sea. How mysterious and beautiful is the sea! how infinitely variable! It is never the same, never, not from one moment to the next, always in the process of change, always becoming something different and new.

In a recent development, in the same way, Casals argues, we renew ourselves through purposeful work. But he adds an admonition about the complacency of talent, echoing Jack Kerouac’s fantastic distinction between talent and genius. Casals offers aspiring artists of all stripes a word of advice on humility and hard work as the surest path to self-actualization:.

I see no particular merit in the fact that I was an artist at the age of eleven. I was born with an ability, with music in me, that is all. No special credit was due me. The only credit we can claim is for the use we make of the talent we are given. That is why I urge young musicians: “Don’t be vain because you happen to have talent. You are not responsible for that; it was not of your doing. What you do with your talent is what matters. You must cherish this gift. Do not demean or waste what you have been given. Work — work constantly and nourish it.”.

Sources indicate that of course the gift to be cherished most of all is that of life itself. One’s work should be a salute to life.

Hence Ray Bradbury’s famous proclamation that he never worked a day in his life — further testament to the magic made possible by discerning your vocation.

Sources indicate that casals lived and worked for another four years, dying eight weeks before his ninety-seventh birthday. Joys and Sorrows remains an invigorating read — a rare glimpse into the source of this creative and spiritual vitality of unparalleled proportions.

Your Intuition Is Smarter Than You Think

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change intends at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous. Or you may feel drawn toward certain people or places without quite knowing why, only to discover later that those connections opened doors to fresh opportunities.

Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach. Other times, they show up as a quiet sense of simply knowing what to do. Whether they’re instantaneous or linger over time, they may be signs of your intuition in action.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you. Over time, this practice of self-awareness can become a habit that helps you live more authentically and fully.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world. Our body’s sensory networks are always at work gathering information from our environment, finding patterns from past experiences, and directing our present-day thinking and decisions.

Through our senses, our nervous system gathers information and sends signals to the brain. Regions like the amygdala help us rapidly detect potential threats, while the prefrontal cortex, which handles complex reasoning and decision-making, helps us interpret information more deliberately.

Research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

According to recent reports, that first, quick assessment happens remarkably fast. For instance, research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

Industry observers note that intuition differs from instinct, which involves automatic responses that can help protect us from danger, including reactions like fight, flight, or freeze. While instinctive responses are largely automatic, intuition draws on our past life experiences and learned patterns to help us make sense of what we encounter in daily life. Although both can feel immediate, intuitive judgments are not always accurate and may also reflect learned biases or assumptions.

Intuition can feel like a gut feeling that is hard to put into words. This is because our brain is able to look for patterns between old memories and present-day situations, using useful takeaways from the past to guide us now. This process can also include implicit, unconscious memories that we may have thought we’d forgotten.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?”.

In a recent development, if the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?” Part of the explanation lies in the gut-brain axis, the complex communication network connecting our brain and digestive system. The walls of our digestive tract contain a network of millions of neurons that make up the enteric nervous system, or ENS.

Recent findings suggest that the ENS is often called our “second brain” because it can regulate many digestive functions independently of the central nervous system. Through the gut-brain axis, digestive processes can also interact with systems involved in mood and emotion. Research has linked gastrointestinal inflammation and changes in gut function with symptoms of depression and anxiety. Most of the body’s serotonin is also produced in the digestive tract, although it doesn’t directly enter the brain. Researchers are still exploring the complex relationship between gut health and mental well-being.

This gut-brain connection helps explain why we might experience a sinking feeling in the pit of our stomach when something doesn’t feel quite right.

All day long, our minds are hard at work integrating rational thought with emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ helps us to become aware of and understand both our emotions and those of others. It’s a type of intelligence we can develop through emotion regulation practice, expanding our emotional vocabulary, and approaching feelings as clues to something instead of an end product.

To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively.

According to recent reports, EQ can help us manage stress, notice our assumptions, and respond more thoughtfully to difficult emotions, such as those that arise after a tense conversation. It helps us pause and remain mindful during challenging moments, and also as we choose our next steps. Developing emotional intelligence may also support our ability to recover from stressful experiences.

In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), combining emotional awareness with rational thinking is known as accessing our wise mind. To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively. Instead of automatically acting on our first reaction, we can ground ourselves while tackling emotionally painful situations.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected. As the ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” suggests, self-knowledge is an notable part of wisdom. By understanding our deeper motivations, core needs, and cherished values, we can make more intentional decisions that reflect who we are and what matters most to us.

Industry observers note that family systems therapist Virginia Satir connected personal authenticity to congruence between our internal reality and outward actions. This alignment can support our emotional well-being and help us act in ways that reflect our values. Incongruence, however, may leave us with a nagging sense that things are not quite right. Noticing incongruence in real time can help us to adjust and choose to do what feels more authentic to us and who we wish to be.

Sometimes, traumatic experiences can make it harder to recognize or trust our intuition, particularly when painful memories leave us feeling fearful or unsafe. Common trauma responses, such as hypervigilance to danger, will tax our nervous system, making it difficult to access the balanced perspective of our wise mind.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks.

According to recent reports, trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks. Similarly, depression can affect our self-esteem and confidence, informing how we interpret new situations as more negative. Holding hope for a better future might require noticing the positive patterns that run through our lives, and accessing support to process what we have gone through.

Sources indicate that social pressure can also make us second-guess ourselves. For example, growing up with family expectations to defer to others and put their needs first might make us believe that prioritizing our own needs is selfish. Similarly, other people’s ideas of what success looks like can make us overlook our own aspirations, such as the desire to pursue a different career path.

Recent findings suggest that we may become more aware of these pressures as we get older. Hospice nurse Bronnie Ware identified five common regrets her patients shared toward the end of their lives:.

These reflections offer a reminder of the importance of making choices that align with what matters most to us.

Getting to know ourselves—our preferences, desires, and even dreams—requires making time to turn inward. A helpful practice for building the habit of self-reflecting is time in peaceful solitude. Time alone may encourage mind-wandering and daydreaming, activities associated with the brain’s default mode network, which plays a role in reflection, imagination, and our sense of self.

Quiet may even have benefits for brain health. In one study, mice exposed to periods of silence developed more immature neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory and learning. Though similar effects haven’t been established in humans, the presence of young neurons in the mice is a sign of brain plasticity. And while quiet moments may sometimes feel boring, they can also create space for reflection, creativity and new ideas.

Other practices, such as spending time in nature, journaling, meditation, engaging in spiritual reflection, and limiting technology, may also strengthen our intuition and self-awareness, as we remember who we are and what we care about the most.

In a recent development, clarity about our personal values is another entryway to deepening intuition. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values help guide meaningful action and provide direction as we navigate life’s uncertainties. They can guide our daily actions much like an inner compass would—keeping us focused on long-term goals.

Knowing our values helps us remember how we want to show up during challenging times and stay grounded when stress feels overwhelming. Values can take many forms, from nurturing relationships, to cultivating personal qualities, or finding greater joy and fulfillment in everyday life. Naming your values and writing them down may help you distinguish between choices rooted in what matters to you and those driven primarily by fear, particularly when clarity feels hard to find.

Psychotherapy can provide an intentional, supportive space where you can go inward. Therapy can also help us explore how past experiences shape our reactions, making it easier to distinguish familiar emotional patterns from what we’re noticing in the present. There are many evidence-based therapies that can help support trauma recovery, managing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and building a stronger sense of self:.

Each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves.

According to recent reports, thinking back to the gut feelings we began with—the caution that turned out to be right, and the inner pull that led toward new possibilities—we can see how these experiences may reflect more than coincidence. Instead, they’re signs that our nervous system, emotional intellect, mental pattern-finding, and lived experience are all working together to shape our perceptions and decisions.

It has been revealed that learning to trust our intuition’s guidance can take practice, particularly if difficult experiences have caused us to doubt it. But each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves. Over time, what once felt like a faint signal may become a steady, recognizable voice that helps us move forward with greater confidence. Our capacity for intuitive wisdom is always there, and the invitation is simply to listen.

Marian Ting, LMFT, is a therapist and writer specializing in mood disorders, complex trauma, and AAPI mental health. She is pursuing a PhD in depth psychology at Pacifica Graduate Institute, with research interests in the synergies between self-compassion and authentic selfhood. Her writing has been published by Psychotherapy Networker, the Anxiety and Depression Association of America, and Psychedelic Support, among others. She believes beauty and struggle can coexist, and that honest self-reflection is a form of healing.

Breaking: Shanghai’s art week finds buyers in a selective market

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar.
  • “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing.
  • Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and upcoming spaces, including three new galleries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.

“I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.

Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and upcoming spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.

It has been revealed that “Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” says Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”.

Hsu states he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this fresh era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”.

Jae Pil Eun's Night Walking, showing at Hang Over.

Courtesy of the artists and SYSTEMA © SYSTEMA, 2026.

Industry observers note that along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the new boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.

Industry observers note that the 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a fresh acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.

Sources indicate that at West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.

Visitor at West Bund Art & Design 2026.

Courtesy of West Bund Art & Design.

Sources indicate that dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she indicates.

In a recent development, hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.

At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.

Industry observers note that also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.

Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, claims that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.

According to recent reports, he suggests that the growth of fresh art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang indicates, adding that Shanghai remains an notable entry point for collectors from across mainland China.

It has been revealed that hsu indicates the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”.

#10355. Vinny Ferraro: Healing Our Pain with Loving-Kindness

Vinny Ferraro: Healing Our Pain with Loving-Kindness

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it?
  • We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally.
  • Sources indicate that add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it? Generally, when we come into contact with something painful or scary, our habitual tendency is to push it away, and to try to get away from it out of self-preservation. This is not your fault. This is biology.

We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally. It’s hard for us to imagine that the things we’ve been battling with our whole lives could be sources of awakening. And it’s so easy to judge our experiences, essentially holding it against ourselves that we are the way we are.

Sources indicate that add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture. Maybe we worry we’re being self-indulgent or even come to see ourselves as inconveniences. It’s so easy to slip into judgment.

Sources indicate that with compassion practice we open up to this tender space. And when that opening happens, we find there’s actually room for the life that’s right here, right now. So, I ask you to go easy on yourself as we venture into this territory of giving ourselves compassion.

What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves?

We come by it all so honestly. But let’s explore: What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves? And what does it really feel like when we wage that war? How much are our experiences bringing to us, and how much are we bringing to our experiences?

Recent findings suggest that consider this: Our response to whatever arises is where we put our attention—that’s what we actually have influence over. We can’t control what arises. We do have some power over where we place our attention.

Industry observers note that many practitioners talk about this in terms of the “second arrow.” That’s when we take something that’s already difficult and multiply that by our resistance to it. And this can be far more painful than the initial feeling itself.

This is the formula: Experience x Resistance = Suffering.

So, how do we hold ourselves with some compassion? “Suffering” is a really major word. In light of all that’s going on in the world, it’s easy to feel like we can dismiss what we’re dealing with personally. But I think we have to include ourselves and whatever difficulties we’re dealing with. The mind is always saying, “Well, at least, you know, at least…”—and you fill in the blank. At least it’s not this, at least it’s not that. I don’t know about you, but I can feel kind of bullied into gratitude when I’m not willing to meet what’s difficult with some compassion. Let’s accept, then, that resistance is normal. Resistance gets to be here, too.

Industry observers note that pain can be in our lives in countless ways—and all of it is difficult. Each one of us has been touched by grief, loss, countless struggles. Those things in and of themselves are difficult for many of us to navigate. But even harder than those things is when we regard what has happened, or is happening, as our fault.

We don’t have to defend our pain or judge ourselves. I see it with my two-year-old son. Sometimes he’s just screaming. Something is just really, really bothering him. It doesn’t matter what it is. I know what he needs. He needs a hug. He needs to be held. He needs care. He needs loving attention.

Sources indicate that that’s what we’re going to do in this practice: hold ourselves with that same kind of care. We’re going to allow ourselves to kiss our own wounds the way we would for anyone we care about.

We start with a willingness to have contact with the pain and soften to it, not resist it. We do that by tuning into our body and the sensations that are present. Is there a temperature shift? A throbbing? Is it moving? Is there a centre; are their edges? Are there places that it’s not?

Industry observers note that if it becomes overwhelming, we can allow our awareness to go to the part of our experience that’s not activated. We can visit where this pain lives in our bodies, and we can come back to a place of calm if it gets to be too much.

According to recent reports, bringing our curiosity to this is key. Not “why is this happening to me?” or the story we might be building around it, but what is the felt sense of this pain? This is the power of mindfulness—the ability to cultivate a clearer view of what’s coming up and therefore not be blindsided by it or lost in it.

It has been revealed that we’re looking for two components in this practice, then: willingness and seeing clearly. Simply put, when we bring compassion home to include ourselves, our job is to honor the hurt. This isn’t easy. In fact, it’s very rare for us to meet ourselves in that place. But if we don’t, we’re losing out on living a considerable portion of our lives.

As we talked about last week, the plan here is to widen our circle of care as we go. We started with those dearest to us; now we’re going focus on ourselves. Next week we will hold neutral people in mind and then we’ll hold everyone, including difficult people. I love the sequence, but sometimes I feel like when I’m practicing, I can be all four of those categories of people. Sometimes I’m an easy person to care about. Sometimes it’s difficult to hold myself with compassion. Sometimes I feel pretty neutral.

I encourage you to reflect on when you feel you need love the most. For me, it’s particularly when I mess up. And when we don’t feel like we can meet ourselves, isn’t that when we really see what kind of lovers we are? Is it conditional—is it as long as I act right? What we want to do here is widen the berth of where we’re willing to meet ourselves.

According to recent reports, I want to re-emphasize here: It’s important not to use any part of the practice to judge ourselves. What we’re trying to do is give ourselves a pardon. This is how we can meet ourselves where we feel most unmet.

I find it helpful to note what’s arising as I’m doing this compassion practice. It helps me to see better what my relationship is to that pain. This also helps me to see this as something that’s passing through my awareness. It’s not who I am. I find that distinction very helpful.

In a recent development, to put it another way, we’re trying not to take any of this personally. We realize we can practice with just about anything if we’re not taking it personally. Whether it’s stress, frustration, pain: nothing has to be outside our care. Maybe we feel like we’ve been through too much pain, or not enough—it doesn’t really matter why we’re in pain, just that we can acknowledge that there is stuff that is painful.

It has been revealed that remember, too, that we’re inviting spaciousness around this pain we’re finding. The pain is not the only thing happening here. This is the alchemy of presence. It helps us approach the very difficulties that we’ve been desperately trying to avoid so that they can become the sources of our awakening, of our wisdom, of equanimity.

OK, let’s stop reading the menu and eat some of the food.

According to recent reports, read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.

Be on the lookout for where compassion arises in your life, in the day to day. Locate where compassion arises naturally and where it could use some cultivation. Try spending some time each day reflecting on your heart’s intention in this practice.

Vinny Ferraro has been a practitioner of insight meditation (vipassanā) since the early 1990s. He is a co-Founder of the Dharma Punx and co-Guiding Teacher of Against the Stream Buddhist Meditation Society. He is also a nationally recognized leader in designing and implementing interventions for at-risk adolescents and is currently Senior Trainer for Mindful Schools. In 1987, he began leading groups in drug rehabilitation centers, juvenile halls, and halfway houses. In 2001, he began teaching for Challenge Day, a nationally recognized, social & emotional learning program, eventually becoming their Director of Training and leading workshops for over 110,000 youth on four continents. Vinny is also a board member and former Training Director of the Mind Body Awareness Project and is the principal author of MBA’s mindfulness-based curriculum for incarcerated youth. Vinny has received national media coverage for his work with adults and youth; his work is the subject of the MTV series “If You Really Knew Me…”.

VS/Goods pairs a warm-stone web design with a dark asset shelf, floating award cards, and interactive mockups built for Figma and Jitter.

Born out of a few templates the team built for Jitter that turned out to be too much fun to stop, VS/Goods skips the usual sterile filter grid. Instead, the storefront greets visitors with a fanned stack of editorial portraits and a clean top bar holding just Menu, All assets, and Account.

Scroll past the opening stack and the page flips from bright white to charcoal dark. Here, tilted pastel cards flash recognition from Awwwards, Motion Design Awards, The Webby Awards, FWA, and CSS Design Awards above a crisp headline. It's a quick credibility beat, and it sets up the dark asset shelf right below it.

That shelf treats each template like a playable preview rather than a flat thumbnail. Cards for Typography, Animated Screens, Animated Mobile Screens, and Rotating Cards sit side by side with clear euro pricing and bright pink Try For Free buttons. You don't have to guess how a file moves before clicking in. Further down, the background warms into an oatmeal tone for the community wall, where softly masked project tiles orbit headlines like Real projects, real energy and All created with our mockups.

Even the footer refuses to sit still. A full-width VS/Goods wordmark with its wavy flag emblem spans the dark canvas above a rotating analog watch dial stamped with the line Move Fast Design Right. Together, the pacing between light editorial sections and dark product shelves gives this web design a rhythm that matches the motion assets it sells. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Norfolk Coast is one of the UK’s best-loved and most at-risk tourist destinations. Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, the region is also home to Sites of Special Scientific Interest, National Nature Reserves, Marine Conservation Zones, a Biosphere Reserve and Heritage Coast. A collection of protected landscapes, united through their biodiversity and fragility. Lantern was appointed to bring these organisations together and better define and promote their common goals to preserve, restore and enhance the local life, landscapes and wildlife of the Norfolk Coast.

We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a latest visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.

Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes.

Industry observers note that to fully understand what makes Norfolk so special and distinct, we embarked on a four-day immersion trip as a team. We hiked, cycled, bird watched, and conducted several interviews with local families and visitors.

It was important for us to discover the genuine essence of Norfolk and what it means for the local community and stakeholders who call it home, as well as identifying the key areas that require greater protection.

In a recent development, norfolk’s coastal landscapes, seascapes and communities have rhythms like a heartbeat. They move across millennia, change with the seasons, and even differ day to day. Waterways widen and wander. Wildlife migrates and hibernates. Farmland flourishes and lies fallow. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. Often wild yet sometimes serene.

Our newly introduced strategy celebrates this wild, natural backdrop and all that defines it; land and sea, nature and community, they all live together in gentle harmony. And like every living thing, this delicate place deserves to be respected and protected.

Inspired by the sweeping landscapes of Norfolk’s coast and creeks we brought together the N and C of the brand name creating a unique symbol, paired with a visual language that’s full of energy and alive with nature.

Reflected through the interplay of type, image and illustration, we put the audience deep into the experience. To further reflect the landscape we directed an off-season photoshoot, encouraging sustainable exploration throughout the year.

Recent findings suggest that A suite of illustrations capture key essences from our findings and strategy along with unique wildlife and nature found in Norfolk. We utilise these within patches and stamps reflecting the positive adventures we want to encourage people to experience.

It’s Selfish, It’s Hokey, and I’ll Lose My Edge: 3 Half-Truths About Self-Compassion

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’m a late adopter of a lot of things.
  • Industry observers note that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion?
  • In a recent development, we think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’m a late adopter of a lot of things. It took me two years to get an iPhone, a lot of convincing to wear AirPods (which I still call ear pods despite my son’s cringe), and it took me even longer to drink the “self-compassion” Kool-Aid. (Which I guess I drank because I wrote a book on how to practice self-compassion daily!).

Industry observers note that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion? I believed three things about self-compassion that turned me off. But I’ve since learned, they are really only half-truths.

In a recent development, we think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused. Yet the research shows that when you practice self-compassion, you are more likely to:.

Industry observers note that if you are a parent, you probably know this firsthand. When you practice caring for yourself, you are less likely to have your stress spill over onto your kids. But there is a half-truth to self-compassion making you selfish.

In other words, if you are worried that self-compassion will make you selfish, focus more on how giving yourself compassion will help you be of service to others. One body-based practice I like to do with this concept is a simple breathing exercise:.

Breathing in, I take in care and understanding.Breathing out, I send out care and understanding.

There is a large body of research showing that self-compassion actually helps you perform better, not worse.

Sources indicate that self-compassion helps you stay on track with your wisest values and goals. The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion you may choose to lose your edge a little…in good ways.

As you learn to listen more to your body and stop berating yourself for mistakes, you naturally may want to give up on pushing yourself in ways that are harmful. I’ve lost my edge when it comes to having to run every day, getting every email returned in a timely manner, and making the perfect dinner for my family (hello Trader Joe’s frozen aisle!) … and that’s a good thing.

Industry observers note that when my clients are struggling with whether or not they should push themselves at something, I ask them to do what contemplative leader Stephen Batchelor suggested to me: Drop the question into your belly. If you struggle with self-criticism or rigid rules, your belly is likely to have a more compassionate answer than your head!

Industry observers note that it can feel uncomfortable to say nice things to yourself, and sometimes downright cheesy. I rarely recommend clients cheer themselves on with the “Good job” or “Way to go!” statements that some motivational coaches suggest.

Sources indicate that self-compassion is relating to yourself in a way that is encouraging, warm, realistic, and just right for you. You don’t need to recite a list of loving-kindness mantras or put your hand on your heart if you find those practices hokey. Sometimes self-compassion is as simple as noticing the part of you that is scared and being with it a little longer.

The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion, you just might start to adopt some hokey platitudes toward yourself. But hey, they are platitudes for a good reason, right?

Sources indicate that to learn more about how to bring self-compassion into your daily life, read The Self-Compassion Daily Journal by Dr. Diana Hill or listen to the Wise Effort Podcast.

Recent findings suggest that diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill.

Originally named “Hồn Đất Việt” — translated as “Viet’s Ceramic Soul” — this museum embodies his remarkable legacy. Vũ Đức Thắng gained widespread recognition for his spectacular creation of 12 remarkably genuine pottery boots, earning the Guinness Record in 2013. His artistic skills include a collection of modern artworks highlighted by two unique techniques: color-changing ceramic glaze and intricate three-dimensional sculpting. These methods display his mastery and creativity in ceramic art.

In a recent development, we carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a fresh look for the museum. This involved giving the museum a new name and creating a unique custom typeface MN Vũ Thắng with “pottery-shoes-soul” inktrap touches. We wanted to echo his process and masterpieces into the content system.

The brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a fresh, clean photography style. A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor plan layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

In a recent development, we simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

Collaboratively, we aimed to assemble the Bát Tràng Museum towards a more contemporary style while preserving its rich heritage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027. Housed in the university’s fresh Triton Center, the Strauss Family Gallery will include four indoor exhibition spaces and an outdoor sculpture terrace. Free and open to the public, the Strauss will host exhibitions, commissions, artist residencies and public programmes that encourage collaboration between artists and UC San Diego researchers and scholars.

Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential. "The Strauss represents a long-term commitment that the university is making to contemporary art and sees it as an integral part of the university's intellectual and public life," she states.

In a recent development, in 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego. (Matthew, who made his money in real estate, died the following year.) Represented artists in the gift include Carrie Mae Weems, Fred Wilson, Zhang Huan and Sabine Moritz.

The Strauss’s upcoming David and Claire Guggenheim Gallery will serve as the public entrance and a space for exhibitions, gatherings and an artist-in-residence programme focused on digital artists, while the two-story Gray Box will accommodate large-scale sculpture, moving-image installations and performances.

The 3,043-sq.-ft Black Box will be equipped for immersive video, sound, sculpture and performance; and the White Cube will provide a more conventional gallery setting for works from the Strauss Family Foundation, travelling exhibitions and collaborations with collections in San Diego and beyond.

Sources indicate that taylor calls the Strauss the first "ground-up museum" at UC San Diego. Pointing to existing spaces on campus like the Mandeville Art Gallery (open for nearly 60 years) and a black-box theatre in the music department, she says the Strauss will strive to be part of the landscape of both the campus and San Diego at large. But the Strauss will play a unique role—with commissions, curatorial research and exhibitions in collaboration with artists from across the globe.

UC San Diego’s Stuart Collection, which includes sculptures installed across campus, has already established a public art presence at the university. The Strauss will now give artists a dedicated space for exhibitions, commissions and research.

In a recent development, “We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve," Taylor says. "The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom.".

Industry observers note that taylor's greater vision is to engage the community through public programming and student involvement. The Strauss looks to engage both established and emerging artists, particularly in the digital space, and support the development of their work. "We're looking at how we can bring artistic inquiry into university teaching and research," Taylor says.

Recent findings suggest that this could include incorporating exhibitions and artistic methodologies into existing courses, giving students opportunities to participate in curatorial research and creative projects, and developing collaborations across the university. Taylor points to potential partnerships with UC San Diego’s Qualcomm Institute, the Interdisciplinary Computing and the Arts programme, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Goeddel Family Technology Sandbox as examples of the range of possibilities.

"We see the Strauss as more of a platform than a container for a collection," Taylor says. "We do have a collection, but our goal is to be a platform for research and critical inquiry—and for challenging assumptions.".
